title: Priv EKS control plane: Terraform fleet seeder module
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Build a reusable Terraform module (fleet-seeder) to reliably bootstrap Redwood Private EKS control planes across customer VPCs. This module should be minimal, idempotent, and focused on the first-control-plane lifecycle: create IAM roles and encrypted secrets, provision the EKS control plane with secure defaults, run post-provision health probes, and emit telemetry for provisioning success/failure. It must be safe to re-run during CI and during controlled rollback/upgrade flows.
background: Current provisioning is a collection of ad-hoc terraform stacks and one-off scripts. That approach complicates audits, makes upgrades risky, and results in inconsistent metrics (time-to-ready, failure modes). We need a single module used by our control plane bootstrapper and by customer onboarding pipelines that enforces guardrails: KMS-backed secrets, ephemeral bootstrap roles, preflight validations (CIDR overlap, quota checks), and a deterministic canonical resource layout.
goals: Provide a single, versioned Terraform module that teams and automated systems can use to seed EKS control planes in customer VPCs
Ensure idempotency: safe re-apply during failures and for reconciliation runs
Surface clear provisioning telemetry and structured failures to Console and onboarding logs
Include built-in health checks and a lightweight recovery path (recreate ephemeral bootstrap resources, rerun validations)
non_goals: Full lifecycle management of worker/node pools (out of scope for this module)
Complex cluster add-ons (CNI customizations beyond secure defaults)
deliverables: Concourse/GHA job templates for safe re-applies and canary seeding
Post-provision health probe scripts and Prometheus/OTEL metrics emitted
Confluence runbook: failure modes and manual recovery steps
Integration tests (kitchen-terraform / terratest) exercising idempotent re-runs
acceptance_criteria: Module exposes a small set of inputs: vpc_id, subnets, kms_key_arn, bootstrap_role_arn, cluster_name, tags
Module completes a full control-plane create in staging within SLA (<= 15 minutes) and emits provisioning.status = SUCCESS to metrics
Re-running terraform apply after an injected failure returns to desired state without resource duplication or leaked secrets
Health probes verify API server reachability, control-plane nodes Ready, certificate rotation fields present
PR with module code reviewed by infra and security, and a security review checklist marked complete
implementation_notes: Design the module with small, composable child modules (iam, kms-bindings, eks-controlplane, post-probe). Use Terraform 1.6+ and the provider constraint patterns we already use. Avoid provider aliasing sprawl—accept an optional assumable_bootstrap_role ARN which the CI runner can use to perform initial creates. Add explicit destroy protections toggles in inputs to prevent accidental tear-down. Keep state remote and documented in the runbook.
tasks: Implement iam submodule with principal-of-least-privilege policy templates
Wire KMS key usage and grant creation patterns for cross-account encryption (optional)
Implement eks-controlplane resource with lifecycle and timeouts tuned for our provisioning profile
Add post-provision probe that runs kubectl (via kubeconfig) and validates pod readiness and control-plane health
Write terratest scenarios: fresh create, simulated partial failure (API error), re-apply idempotency
Add OTEL metric instrumentation and Console ingestion hook for provisioning events
Create Confluence runbook and GHA job examples for canary seeding
risks: KMS cross-account grant logic could be complex for customer-managed keys and cause access failures
EKS control plane API rate limits could slow down provisioning at scale during fleet onboarding
Misconfigured timeouts can lead to Terraform hanging on control plane readiness
Improper IAM scoping might open broader privileges—security review required
mitigations: Add explicit tests around KMS grant scenarios and fallback to provider-managed keys
Introduce rate-limiting backoff and retry in orchestration layer; document expected throughput
Set conservative resource timeouts and fail-fast on known transient errors; provide advice in runbook
Mandate a security PR checklist and require a separate reviewer from the security team before merge
